Do the greats really serve better when it matters most? The goal for clutchserve is to allow tennis fanatics who want to put the term “clutch” to test. It packages point-by-point data on men’s professional matches with an interactive dashboard to compare how players serve on pressure points (break points and optionally deuce) with how they serve on every other point. You can also visualise a player’s progression over time to see whether they’ve become more clutch across their career.

Installation

You can install the development version of clutchserve from GitHub with:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("ETC5523-2026/etc5523-assignment-4-pang0023-arch")

Launch the app 

clutchserve::run_app()

The app shows every player as a dot on a funnel chart, compared with a typical player. Use the sidebar to filter by surface, years and choose what counts as a reliable pressure point and set that as the minimum number of pressure points. Click a player to see how their serve under pressure has changed over time.

Example

pressure_gap() summarises each player’s point performance of each match (including pressure points and normal points).

library(clutchserve)

pressure_gap(serve_pressure) |>
  summary()

Data

serve_pressure has one row per player per recorded match: 14,570 rows of men’s matches from 1990 onwards. It comes from Match Charting Project by Jeff Sackmann, licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. The packaged data carries the same licence. The script that downloads and cleans it is in data-raw/serve_pressure.R.

The matches are recorded by volunteers, so famous players and big matches are overrepresented. Results describe the recorded matches, not every match a player has played. This data should not be taken as a random sample of professional tennis.
